title: My day
verifiedBy: Claude Fable 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: ONE Italian present covers BOTH English presents: mangio is "I eat" and "I am eating" alike, and which one it is comes from the sentence, never from the form. Italian has its own progressive (sto mangiando) for what is happening this second; it belongs to a later level, and nothing here needs it.
The present is one stem plus an ending, in all three verb classes: parlo · parli · parla (-are); bevo · bevi · beve (-ere); dormo · dormi · dorme (-ire). The tu ending is -i in every one of them.

Daily verbs carry a little pronoun in front, and it changes with the person: mi alzo · ti alzi · si alza. English "I get up" has nothing there at all, so the dropped mi is the commonest slip in this module.

A time word normally goes in FRONT of the sentence — Di mattina mangio il pane, Ogni giorno parlo con Anna — and can also stand at the end. What it never needs is an extra preposition Italian has not written.
The article is what turns a day into a habit: il lunedì means "on Mondays", every Monday, while a bare lunedì is one particular Monday. English does that job with a plural -s.
The clock runs on alle, a + le squeezed into one word: alle sette, alle otto. Italian fuses a preposition and a following article like this wherever the two meet.
si — the little pronoun of si alza and si chiama — is M2's sì with the accent taken off, and the two are different words. The accent is never optional in either direction.

sentences.glossEn: lit. "Speak Italian every day" — the "I" is inside parlo

words.note: parlare — to speak, the first of the three verb classes. The stem stays and the ending names the person: parlo (I) · parli (you) · parla (he, she). With a language after it the article drops: parlo italiano, not parlo l'italiano.
every day. ogni is followed by a SINGULAR noun — ogni giorno, never ogni giorni — which is the opposite of what English "every day" would suggest if you translated it piece by piece.

sentences.trap: This one sentence is both English presents at once: "I speak Italian every day" and "I am speaking Italian every day" are the same Italian. There is nothing to add for the -ing.
sentences.sound: PAR-lo. The r is one tap of the tongue and the l is clear and forward, never the dark l of English "full".

variations.cue: Do you speak Italian?
variations.changed: -o → -i: the ending moves to you, and nothing is added to ask

variations.cue: I don't speak Italian every day
variations.changed: non in front of the verb; the time phrase stays where it was

variations.cue: Every day I speak Italian
variations.changed: the time phrase moved to the front — Italian is content either way

mistake.why: ogni takes a singular noun: ogni giorno. The plural belongs to tutti i giorni, which says the same thing another way.

sentences.usage: Saying what you do habitually — the frame the whole module is built on.
sentences.mnemonic: ogni counts them one at a time, so the noun stays singular.

words.note: alzarsi — literally "to raise oneself". The little pronoun is part of the verb and changes with the person: mi alzo (I) · ti alzi (you) · si alza (he, she). English "get up" has nothing in that slot, which is why it is the piece most often dropped.

"At seven" — alle is a + le fused into one word, and the le is there because the hours are feminine and plural (le sette, le otto). Taught whole: the clock always takes alle, except for one o'clock, which takes all'una.

sentences.trap: Two things are here that English does not have: a pronoun inside the verb, and a fused a + le in front of the hour. Neither is optional.
sentences.sound: AL-tso — the z is a "ts". mi runs straight into it, so the pair comes out as one word. In alle sette both doubled consonants are held: a single one would give ale and sete, which are other words.

variations.cue: Do you get up at seven?
variations.changed: mi → ti and the verb ending with it — both halves move together

variations.cue: He gets up at eight
variations.changed: mi → si for a third person, and another hour after alle

variations.cue: I don't get up at seven
variations.changed: non goes in front of the whole verb, pronoun included

mistake.why: The mi is not decoration — it is part of the verb. Mi alzo alle sette.

sentences.usage: The first line of anyone's day, and the one a language exchange asks for first.
sentences.mnemonic: alzarsi raises YOURSELF, so the little pronoun goes with you.

sentences.cue: In the morning I eat bread

words.note: "In the morning", as a habit rather than one particular morning. Taught whole, because the di inside it is not the di of sono di Roma — it is doing a job English gives to "in".
The present of mangiare (M3): mangio (I) · mangi (you) · mangia (he, she). It is "I eat" and "I am eating" at once — Italian has one present where English has two.

sentences.trap: English drops the article for a kind of food — "I eat bread" — and Italian keeps it: mangio il pane. It is M1's rule again, in a new place.
sentences.sound: mat-TI-na, with the double t held, and MAN-jo, where gi is the j of "jam" and the i is not a syllable of its own.

variations.cue: In the morning I eat a pizza
variations.changed: swap what is eaten — the time phrase in front is untouched

variations.cue: Do you eat bread in the morning?
variations.changed: -o → -i and the time phrase moved to the end: both moves are free

variations.display: Non mangio il pane di mattina
variations.cue: I don't eat bread in the morning
variations.changed: non in front of the verb, and everything else holds

mistake.why: A kind of thing keeps its article in Italian: mangio il pane. Bare pane would be asking for some particular quantity of it.

sentences.usage: Describing a routine — what you do, and when.
sentences.mnemonic: di mattina is a habit; una mattina would be one morning.

sentences.cue: In the evening I study Italian

words.note: "In the evening", the habitual one, built exactly like di mattina and taught whole for the same reason. Italian counts the evening from mid-afternoon, so di sera starts earlier than English "in the evening" does.
The present of studiare (M3): studio (I) · studi (you) · studia (he, she). Unlike parlare with a language, studiare keeps the article: studio l'italiano.

sentences.trap: parlo italiano drops the article and studio l'italiano keeps it. That is not a rule about languages — it is a difference between the two verbs, and it is worth learning as a pair.
sentences.sound: SE-ra, one tapped r, and STU-dyo — the -dio is one syllable, DYO, not dee-oh.

variations.cue: In the evening I study every day
variations.changed: two time phrases, one at each end, and neither needs a preposition

variations.cue: Do you study Italian in the evening?
variations.changed: -o → -i, the time phrase at the end, and a question mark to ask

variations.cue: In the morning I study Italian
variations.changed: swap the half of the day — the frame is the same

mistake.why: studiare keeps the article: studio l'italiano. It is parlare that drops it — parlo italiano.

sentences.usage: Saying when you do the thing you are trying to get better at.
sentences.mnemonic: You SPEAK a language bare and STUDY it with its article.

sentences.glossEn: lit. "The Monday I-work" — the article makes it every Monday

words.note: The article is what makes it a habit: il lunedì is "on Mondays", every Monday, while a bare lunedì is one particular Monday. The same trick works down the week — il martedì, il mercoledì — and the accent on lunedì is never dropped.
lavorare — to work: lavoro (I) · lavori (you) · lavora (he, she). It is also the noun "work", and the sentence around it is what tells you which.

sentences.trap: English marks the habit with a plural — "on Mondays" — and Italian marks it with the article instead. Drop the il and you have said one specific Monday.
sentences.sound: lu-ne-DEE: the accent marks the last syllable as the stressed one. la-VO-ro is stressed in the middle, and both r's are single taps.

variations.cue: On Saturdays I work
variations.changed: swap the day — the article keeps doing the same job

variations.cue: On Mondays I don't work
variations.changed: non in front of the verb, behind the time phrase

variations.cue: Do you work on Mondays?
variations.changed: -o → -i and the time phrase at the end — nothing else is added to ask

mistake.why: Without the article, lunedì is one particular Monday, which cannot be "every day". For the habit it is il lunedì.

sentences.usage: Laying out a week — which days you work and which you do not.
sentences.mnemonic: The article makes the day a habit: il lunedì, every one of them.

sentences.cue: What time do you get up?

words.note: "At what time", taught whole. Italian asks with the preposition already attached — a che ora — where English can leave it off ("what time do you get up?"), and the answer comes back with alle: alle sette.

sentences.trap: English fronts "do" to ask. Italian fronts only the question phrase, and the verb stays exactly as it was: A che ora ti alzi?
sentences.sound: che is KE — a c before h is always hard. The three words run together: a-ke-O-ra.

variations.cue: What time do you eat?
variations.changed: swap the verb — the question phrase in front never changes

variations.cue: What time do you work?
variations.changed: another verb, and still nothing added to make it a question

variations.cue: I get up at seven
variations.changed: the answer: a che ora is asked with a, and answered with alle

mistake.why: The a is part of the question: A che ora ti alzi? Bare Che ora è? is a different question — it asks what time it is now.

sentences.usage: Arranging to meet, or asking about someone's routine.
sentences.mnemonic: Ask with a, answer with alle.

sentences.cue: I get up early every day

words.note: early. It is an adverb, so it never changes shape — and it sits right after the verb, where molto sits too.

sentences.trap: presto is "early", not "soon-ish" and not "fast": for speed Italian says velocemente, and a presto on its own is "see you soon".
sentences.sound: PRE-sto. The e is close and the s before t is a plain s, never a z.

variations.cue: Do you get up early?
variations.changed: mi → ti with the ending, and the time phrase dropped

variations.cue: I don't get up early
variations.changed: non in front of the whole verb, pronoun included

variations.cue: She gets up early every day
variations.changed: mi → si: a third person's routine, everything else in place

mistake.why: presto belongs beside the verb: Mi alzo presto ogni giorno. The time phrase goes at either end, but the adverb hugs the verb.

sentences.usage: The line that starts every conversation about mornings.
sentences.mnemonic: presto hugs the verb, the way molto does.

sentences.cue: In the evening I drink a coffee

words.note: The present of bere (M3), and the stem is not what the infinitive would predict: bevo (I) · bevi (you) · beve (he, she). Italian keeps a handful of verbs like this, where the plain form has worn down and the present has not.

sentences.trap: bere is the plain form and bevo is the present, and the v appears from nowhere. It is worth learning the pair together rather than deriving one from the other.
sentences.sound: BE-vo, both syllables short and clean, with no glide on the o.

variations.cue: Do you drink a coffee in the evening?
variations.changed: -o → -i, the time phrase to the end, and a question mark

variations.cue: I don't drink coffee in the evening
variations.changed: non in front of the verb, and the article gone with the amount

variations.cue: In the morning I drink a coffee
variations.changed: swap the half of the day — the frame holds

mistake.why: The present of bere is bevo, with a v: Di sera bevo un caffè.

sentences.usage: Talking about habits at the edges of the day.
sentences.mnemonic: bere loses its v in the plain form and finds it again in bevo.

words.note: "On Saturdays", the same habit article as il lunedì. Six days of the week are masculine and take il; only la domenica, Sunday, is feminine.

sentences.trap: The negative and the habit do not interfere with each other: the time phrase stays in front, non stays glued to the verb, and nothing is added between them.
sentences.sound: SA-ba-to, stressed on the first syllable — three light syllables in a row, and none of them swallowed.

variations.cue: On Saturdays I work
variations.changed: drop non and the sentence turns positive

variations.display: Il sabato non mi alzo presto
variations.cue: On Saturdays I don't get up early
variations.changed: another verb behind the same time phrase — non still hugs it

variations.cue: Do you work on Saturdays?
variations.changed: -o → -i, the time phrase at the end, and nothing added to ask

mistake.why: non goes in front of the verb, never after it: Il sabato non lavoro.

sentences.usage: The other half of the working week.
sentences.mnemonic: Six days take il; only la domenica is feminine.

sentences.cue: Every day I speak with Anna

words.note: with. It stays a separate word in front of its noun and does not fuse with a following article the way a, di, in and su do: con il caffè, con la musica.

sentences.trap: Italian fuses most prepositions onto a following article — a + il = al, di + il = del — and con is the one that comfortably does not. con il and con la are written out.
sentences.sound: KON, short, and it leans onto the word after it: con Anna comes out as one breath.

variations.cue: I speak with Anna every day
variations.changed: the time phrase moved to the end — Italian is content either way

variations.display: Non parlo con Anna ogni giorno
variations.cue: I don't speak with Anna every day
variations.changed: non in front of the verb; the phrase behind it is untouched

variations.cue: Do you speak with Anna on Saturdays?
variations.changed: -o → -i and the habit article at the end, asked with nothing added

mistake.why: Speaking WITH someone is con. a would make it speaking TO them, which Italian says as parlo ad Anna and means something narrower.

sentences.usage: Naming who is in your routine, not just what is.
sentences.mnemonic: con keeps its distance: it never fuses with the article.
